utterances.text: Did you see him in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I said that I did. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In what capacity was he working at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: He was shift leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So that's Kolundzija, Dosen, and was there another shift leader, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Could you explain to me what this has to do with my testimony at all, who was shift leader and who wasn't?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I am going to intervene at this point. This is a question that we discussed. You are here to answer questions and not to ask questions yourself. Of course, it is true that you can ask questions if they are pertinent, but this is a matter we discussed, as you understood. So please answer the question you have been asked by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge, can I say something? If I say I want a private session, then I need one. I don't want to name names until we are in private session, because I have to go back to that environment and I want protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have no objection to private session, Your Honour, although I will indicate that, as a matter of public record, there are names on indictments. But it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Let us move into private session, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated during your testimony that Zoran Zigic would go for, I believe you said, water and food. Was that correct, water and food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And in what types or type of vehicle would he go for those commodities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: In a minibus.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And he drove it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: He did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you driven that minibus? Are you familiar with that particular bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I did not drive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Have you seen it inside, for example? Have you seen the layout of the inside of the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no, I didn't see the inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not it was a manual, with a four- or five-speed transmission, or an automatic? Would you happen to know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't go into the minibus. I really don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You also made reference to a motorcycle. What type of motorcycle was it that accused Zigic was riding, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: A small, white, automatic motorcycle popular in our parts. That's why I know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It had the typical hand controls of a regular motorcycle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, hand controls, the regular type of motor. It didn't have any speeds. It was just -- you'd just press the fuel -- like a moped, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know how it operated? I mean, how did you start it and how did you increase -- if you needed to go a little bit faster, how would you do that on that type of a motorcycle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: You would switch it on by pressing the pedal with your leg. I don't know. I never drove a motorcycle like that. I never rode one myself. But I think you would press your foot down and that would make it start. There was a pedal. You would turn the pedal, depress it, and then it would take off; release the fuel, inject the fuel, and it would take off.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And like any motorcycle, you would steer it with your hands, is that correct, like any motorcycle; nothing special about that one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you want to go into private session to answer this, we can do that, but I would like to ask you, please, to tell us exactly what it was you had to do that took you out of Keraterm camp at about 6.00 the evening of the 24th of July - excuse me. I'm sorry - at about 2130 hours on the 24th of July. If you'd like private session indicated, it will just take a minute.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I can answer that question as we are. My mother was ill, so I had to go home, but first I went to have a cup of coffee with some ladies, lady friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where did you have that coffee? After you left Keraterm, you had coffee with some lady friends. Where did you have the coffee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: How can I explain? It was Prvomajska street, if you know it, number 405 at the beginning of the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was it a cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No. It was a private house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And when you say some ladies, were they young ladies; ladies your age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, ladies of my age, yes, my age.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But social, social friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, a friendly visit, me and my colleague and the two of them. How shall I explain that to you? Normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay with your friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: A long time, very long.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you leave the ladies' private home to go to your mom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but my house is about -- well, it's nearby, relatively nearby. I needed 15 minutes to get home. I went and then returned to the same place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was nearby to what? Your home was nearby to the home of the ladies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you stayed there for a fairly long period of time with your lady friends, then you went to your home to see --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- see your mom, and then you went back to see the ladies. And then did you go back immediately to Keraterm after that, after seeing the ladies, or did you go back to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right from seeing the ladies, you went directly back to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes. This is how it was: I went there, had some coffees, visited my mother, saw whether she was all right, whether she needed any help, because my mother has been ill for quite a long time, so I went to see how she was. It was difficult to come by medicine, but she had taken her medicine. She had attacks, and it's an ugly sight to see when she's undergoing one of those attacks. Her jaws trembles and so on. But she said she was all right, and then I went back to my lady friends, and then, about four or five, I returned to Keraterm from my lady friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have a particular indication that night that your mom was in particularly bad shape that would have taken you out of Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, when I went to work she was feeling poorly, so I knew when I left for work that she was feeling poorly, and I wanted to see how she was. But I left exceptionally that night. I didn't usually leave my shifts; I would always work through my whole shift. I would leave my shift only very rarely. I didn't usually do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And so knowing -- are you saying, though, you came to work that day knowing that you would have to leave a bit early? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, when you spoke with your shift leader and indicated that you needed to go and, as you had mentioned on page 28, you got permission, was that the first time, or what time did you actually tell your shift leader that you needed to go? When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I think it was the first time. I said straight away that I had to go, so whether he let me go or not, that wasn't important. I would have gone anyway. I had to go see my mother, and I had to do that. It's something I just had to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But what time did you announce to that person, to the shift leader, that you were going to need to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, when I came on duty, and he said, "Well just tell me so I know," so that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just help me remember: What time did you come on duty that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Between six and seven. I don't remember exactly, between 6 and 7 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you had mentioned that they needed at Keraterm to get some additional staffing, and I think the TO were mentioned in your testimony, that more people were needed. Did you have difficulty with anybody superior to you because you were trying to leave at a time when they were trying to boost their staff? Did that cause any conflict among those assigning work details?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No, and let me tell you why. They took over the night shifts and provided security for Keraterm. We would mostly sleep during the night, if you understand what I'm saying. They provided the security, so we didn't really have much to do, and so for the most part, we rested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, that night, from what you indicated in your direct evidence, they were not resting. There appeared to have been some extraordinary activity. Is that what you came to find when you returned at four in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you were with your lady friends and at your mom's house, can you tell us, please, the distance from Keraterm to your lady friends' house and then your mom's house, the distances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, Keraterm is from those ladies about a kilometre away, and so is my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you were at the ladies' or your mom's between the hours of midnight and roughly four-ish, four in the morning, or returning to Keraterm at four, but you were in the vicinity about a kilometre from Keraterm during that whole period of time, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you hear the bursts of gunfire that were almost non-stop at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, it was like this; let me explain to you to help you understand. I laugh because I knew you'd be asking me that question. I assumed you would, at least. It was like this: When I visited my mother and went back to my lady friends, I was very tired and went to sleep, and in the morning about 4 a.m. I was woken up by the shooting. Now, can you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This Chamber has heard testimony that at the home of Zigic's parents in Cirkin Polje, not too terribly far, the people who were enjoying a garden barbecue heard very distinctly the sound of repeated gunfire for hours on end. I'm curious how perhaps you didn't hear it until the time you just mentioned. Could you maybe help us understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I slept very soundly. When I'm really tired, I don't hear anything. A top could go off, a cannon, and I wouldn't hear it firing. I'm a very sound sleeper when I'm tired.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But you had been drinking coffee for several hours. Coffee is not alcohol.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Doesn't matter. Coffee doesn't make any difference. I can have a cup of coffee now and go straight to sleep right here and now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you got back to Keraterm, were you given any particular orders about what to do? When you arrived, you saw a scene that you said was not the Keraterm that you left earlier that evening. What did you do? How did you react?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, nothing. When I passed by, you saw the way I went, I simply arrived. The commander was there, and he said, "Go to your post," and I went straight to my post. And of course, everybody could see what the situation was like, what the scene was like there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where was your post, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: At the entrance to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you came back, did you have your weapons on, or did you have to get them from some depot in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: You always carried your weapons with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What type of weapon were you carrying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: An automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before you left Keraterm to go visit your lady friends and your mom, can you tell us who was in the camp? Who did you actually see in the way of guards before you left; and when you came back, whom did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Could you explain what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Before you left, let me ask you specifically, before you left, did you see, let's say, Dusko Sikirica at Keraterm before you left, or Zivko Knezevic? Were they there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where would they usually be if they were on the premises? Did they have particular locations where you could find them if you needed to reach them easily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: If they were in the Keraterm compound, then they would be at the weighing-in machine, and you saw where that was. The hut next to the weighing-in machine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: They would be inside the hut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you, did you have any need to stop at that hut before you left at 9.30, or did you just get out because you had to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes. I had to leave my keys there, in the hut.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who was in the hut when you left? Who was actually there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: The shift leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your shift leader, the one you named earlier in your testimony, the same person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you see Zivko Knezevic at all there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had mentioned Mr. Bahonjic who had died as a result, I believe you said, of beatings. At one point he had been taken to the hospital, as I understood it, because he indicated he had something like pains in his stomach. Am I -- did I follow you correctly? He went to the hospital as a result of perceived pains, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, mostly that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know who took him to the hospital and which hospital he went to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I think that he was taken to the hospital in Cirkin Polje. I don't know for sure, but this is the only and the biggest hospital in the area, and I believe he was taken there by the shift leader in his car, a van. I don't know exactly how it was. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you in a position, or do you want to go in closed or private session, to tell us the name of that particular shift leader? Do you want private session for that? I'm going to ask you that question, so you tell us how you want to go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I think we will have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, would it be possible for you to organise your cross-examination in such a way that we could have one private session for every such questions; otherwise, we keep moving into and out of private sessions. I will now order a private session for this purpose, but I just wish you could organise your questioning bearing that in mind, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate your concern. I would like to. It seems there's a sensitivity which will arise periodically, and because the questions flow sometimes one from the other, it will not always be predictable. Apologies for any inconvenience. Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, although Mr. Bahonjic was taken for stomach pains, you are unable to tell us if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Somers, sorry to interrupt you, but you cannot make here any assessment of the reactions of the witness. These are the conditions of the work that we have accepted, so please abstain from any such comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you. I was just trying to indicate that this was a rather unusual sequence for us since I have been with this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Witness, please tell us, if you can, when Mr. Bahonjic, whom you described as having been repeatedly beaten, you may have used the term "continuously" -- do you recall anyone taking him to the hospital after the beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I don't remember after the beatings. I remember only about that particular occasion, because he was complaining of pains and a Muslim came to see me and to tell me to go over to him, which I did, and he really looked terrible. And I went to the duty officer, who then called the commander, Zivko Knezevic, and then he was taken to hospital. He received orders to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There has been a fair amount of testimony about the condition of Mr. Bahonjic. Was it also your observation that he could barely walk after a period of time, he had been so badly beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, he did walk, he could walk, although he had been beaten up. He was all black and blue; that's true. You know how a man who has been beaten up looks. But he could walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could he run? Could he walk fast enough to escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, you know, they could all run, but they didn't dare. He had to escape slowly. There were many people in that dormitory, 400 or 500 people, so he was able to walk past us slowly. We wouldn't see him. I mean, we couldn't observe them all the time. He didn't have to run in order to escape; that's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The condition in which he found himself, you yourself indicated you had to look away, you couldn't watch, you felt sorry for him. Was it pathetic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I felt sorry for all of them, to tell you the truth, but that's the way how he looked. But others looked the same as well. It was nothing special. He could walk with a limp, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And your way of dealing with it was to walk away because it was difficult to look at; is that correct? It was difficult?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I couldn't watch that. Ever since I was in the primary school, when I had to attend a funeral because the father of one of our colleagues was killed in a car accident, and ever since that time, I was simply unable to observe, to watch such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It was your testimony that Bahonjic was in Room 1, but it was also your testimony that Room 1 was for those who were deemed to be less severe, perhaps less severe risks. Maybe you can explain why someone who you said was in Room 1, which was for those lower or less severe risks, would have to be beaten regularly and, in fact, beaten to death.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: He was considered to be dangerous, relatively dangerous, but he was put in Room 1 before my arrival and he stayed there. But I don't know the reason why he was put in Room 1, but perhaps at that time that was the only room that there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You felt sorry for all of those people. Did you hear the screams that permeated the atmosphere at Keraterm from beatings and abuse? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I heard something, but I didn't hear everything. It was a bit further away. I wasn't able to hear everything that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated you took, as one of the four responsibilities, detainees up for interrogation. Did you stand outside the rooms while these persons were being interrogated and perhaps beaten or abused? Did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I stood in front of the door, but I didn't hear anything coming from the inside. I didn't hear any scream or anything of that kind. That I'm perfectly certain about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you observe that the individual whom you may have brought up for interrogation and left behind a closed door and waited for, did you observe those persons to be in the same physical condition when they came out as when they went in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: They were not in the same physical condition. As they entered the room, they were scared and tense, but when they left the room, they were more relaxed. It's like what happened with me when I entered this courtroom for the first time and when I left it. I mean, the difference is huge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In June of 1992, did you hear of any incident involving Zoran Zigic and detainees whom he promised to assist in their release for a sum of Deutschmarks? Did you become aware of that and of the investigation that ensued?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There was no talk at all among any of your colleagues at Keraterm about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: There were some rumours, but I didn't really listen to them. I don't know much about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What type of watch do you have now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: A Seiko watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you acquire that Seiko watch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: A long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Perhaps in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: This is absurd. Do you want me to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like you to answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's really an offence to me to have to respond to this kind of question. I hope you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please answer the question. I don't see it the way you see it. If anyone should ask me what type of watch I'm wearing and where I acquired it, I wouldn't think that it is an insult. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, but she said that I had acquired it in 1992. That is what I believe is an insult for me, because I was in Keraterm in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Witness. It's a question that the Prosecutor is asking of you. She even said "perhaps" or "maybe." You can perhaps correct her, but you have to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No, it was prior to that that I acquired it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: A person by the name of Adnan Filovic was beaten, or claims to have been beaten by you, while in Keraterm in 1996 [sic] for failure to have turned over bread to a detainee --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 1992. Did I say that? I beg your pardon. 1992, for failure to have turned over to a detainee by the name of Senad Kenjar some bread which you were to have promised him in exchange for his Seiko watch in Keraterm. Is that the same Seiko watch you took from Senad Kenjar in exchange for the bread?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the reason that people were detained in Keraterm? What was the purpose of bringing them in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: For the purpose of interrogation as to whether they had taken part in the attack on Prijedor, if they were loyal to the Serb authorities, whether they were involved in arms smuggling, whether they had any weapons, whether they had fought on the other side. That was the purpose of the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So everyone who was brought into Keraterm and detained, and perhaps not released, would have at some point been suspected of some disloyalty to the new Serb government or political entity, or some other form of activity; that would be your explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to distribute Prosecutor's 3/250, please. If you would also be kind enough to put one on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In front of you, Witness DD/6, is a document which does not bear a signature but was taken from the Prijedor collection at the Prijedor Police Station recently, in a seizure not too long ago, and it has a date in the body of it - it is a reference point - and it purports to be composed by Zoran Zigic in connection with an incident you said there were rumours about at Omarska [sic] but that you yourself did not have direct knowledge of. In this statement, which is given to the Ministry of the Interior for the Serbian Republic of BH, Banja Luka, at the Public Security Station Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic. Sorry to interrupt you, Madam Somers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I haven't so far heard Omarska being mentioned at any point in time. The Prosecutor is now mentioning a statement which was given in Omarska. I really don't know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That is an error. It should read "Keraterm." That is my error. Thank you for bringing it to my attention, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At Keraterm. I'm terribly sorry, Witness, if I confused you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This deals with, on 10 June 1992 -- supposedly Zigic says: "I was part of the security at the Keraterm temporary prison. That day, Esad Maroslic was brought in for further processing. I have known that man for years and I know for sure that he is not a nationalist, nor was he involved in anything. I also know that he used to work in Germany and that he has quite a lot of money. I thought of offering to release him for compensation, which I should not have done. He gave me 4.000 Deutschmarks and I released him under the condition that he would not leave his house or courtyard. I resolved to do this because my financial situation is really bad. I have eight members --" some difficulty reading this " -- of the family at home... I sincerely regret this action and I will take full responsibility." My question to you is: If in fact this was compiled by Mr. Zigic, there is a statement that says this man, Maroslic, presumably a Muslim, who is being held in Keraterm, was neither a nationalist nor involved in anything. How can you reconcile holding a man who is not a nationalist or involved in anything in a centre which you indicated was dedicated to ferreting out persons who were a threat to the Serb entity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, the question is based on a statement which is not signed at all. We are not sure about the authenticity of this statement. It's a simple photocopy of a document. And the question is based on an assumption, on a mere hypothesis that the individual in question was not a nationalist and so on and so forth, and how he was arrested and things like that. We don't even know whether the witness has any knowledge about that because no question has been asked of him to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The thrust of my question, Your Honour, was the fact that this witness has indicated the nature of the reasons for detention. And if in fact this document has any merit, it is suggested by a man who claims to have known the individual for years - it says, "I have known that man for years" - that in fact the man was not in the category of persons that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers. Sorry to interrupt you, but the question is "if" the document had been -- no. You always ask two questions. You always have to ask two questions if the document has any value at all, and then later on whether the individual was a nationalist or not. Would you please rephrase your question, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The content of this document, which I am not asking you to vouch for, suggests a premise that a person who is not a nationalist or not involved in anything, which is known or purports to be known to the person writing it or giving it, does not comport or agree with your understanding of why persons were detained in Keraterm. Do you have any notion of how many people may have been in this situation there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but there were quite a few of them. There were all kinds of people there. Some were not guilty of anything, and some were released home, and this is what I already indicated. I'm talking about those in respect of whom it was established that they had not taken part in the attack, that they did not have any weapons, that they had signed the loyalty statement, those were released.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And if this person were not released but had remained there, not being guilty of anything, does that come into conflict with your understanding of why people were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, according to what I -- according to my understanding. But I didn't have any say in that. I didn't take part in the decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have discretion in when you would open and when you would close the dormitory doors; when you would give out water and when you would give out food? Could you be more lenient or more strict in your own discretion, or what were the guidelines for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No, I was not able to decide. It wasn't up to me to issue decisions. I merely received instructions as to the distribution of the food, the unlocking and locking of the dormitories. I would be given the key and told what to do, and that is how it went.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The night of the 24th of July, 1992, did you lock the doors of Room 3? Was that part of your responsibilities before you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes. Regardless of what the room was in question, Room 1, 2, or 3, I would lock them all. I had -- I would receive the key at the gate, went over to the dormitories, locked them up, and then I would take the key back to that hut which was placed there at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So that night, 24th July 1992, you in fact locked the dormitory door and then you left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated it was about 30 degrees centigrade in that room; quite hot. Did you attempt to ask for any relief for the persons who were in that room before you left; extra water, a little ventilation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I said that the outside temperature was 30 degrees. I didn't actually enter the room. We didn't dare go and mix with those detainees, with those people there, if you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So it could have been hotter than 30 degrees inside; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't go there. I didn't go inside, but it could have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're now going to have our usual lunch break because I don't think we can finish the witness before that. How much more time do you think you will need, Mr. Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I want to react. For the purposes of your time, I don't think I will need more than ten minutes. Whether you want me to proceed or whether you think it's better to go and have a break now, it's really up to you. Yes, you also have your questions, of course. But I will be very brief. My questions will be very brief indeed. I just wanted to let you know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't dare ask the interpreters. I don't know what their preferences are, but I think that we will have to work until 1.30, and then we will have worked two hours, and I think this is too much for the interpreters. But anyhow, I think it is always better to have our usual break; otherwise, we will be working under too much pressure. I will now kindly ask the usher to accompany the witness out of the courtroom so that he, too, can have his lunch break. Fifty-minute break. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Deretic, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I believe that the curtains should be up, although it is private -- I mean, it's a protected, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're quite right. Thank you. Mr. Deretic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Witness DD/6, that critical evening, the 24th of July, 1992, when you, in the evening, sometime between 2100 hours and 2130 hours, when you left the Keraterm compound, did your guard post remain void, empty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you -- actually, she showed you an official note of the security commander dated the 4th of July, 1992. Did you ever have occasion to see that official note?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you know of its contents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, it would be advisable if you could give us the exhibit number. That would facilitate our work. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President. It was document number 3/249, Prosecution Exhibit 3/249. It was presented by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: As this is a document dating back to the beginning of July, did you see Zoran Zigic at all during that time frame?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: You also said at the beginning of your testimony that you would see Zoran Zigic in the Keraterm compound driving a minibus and a moped; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: You also said that at that time you had contact with him; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: When you met him, would Zoran Zigic complain to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Would he complain about his injury?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What did he say to you on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: He said that his hand hurt a great deal and that he didn't like having the bandage on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And two more short questions. Witness, I'm not still quite clear on one of the answers you gave to my question, so let me repeat that question. Did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we please go into private session, on second thought, for a few moments, because I'm going to mention a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness DD/6, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: First, I would like to understand a few things better, if you can, for me about it. You mentioned as far as your role was concerned, apparently one of your functions was to prevent, as you said, prevent civilians from getting to the detainees. That was one of your four responsibilities. And in spite of that, people would come in, civilians or others would come in to beat the detainees. That's what I gathered. Did I understand rightly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No, not civilians. They were all wearing uniforms. All the people that came in were in uniform and had weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said exactly they were beaten every day and night by military and reserve police and people coming from outside. Who are these people coming from outside? Anybody would come in to beat anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, those from around Prijedor, from the different units around Prijedor. You didn't know who they were. How can I explain this? They would -- there were various groups from Knin. They were the military and the policemen. They were all in uniform, all these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So anybody in uniform can go and beat anybody, any of the detainees, from anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, they could if we were not able to prevent them, and in those cases, we couldn't prevent them because they were large groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. You said you could not watch it, and you had to move away. That's all you could do? You could not -- was what your -- what was your position in the camp? Were you just a simple guard, or did you have any kind of authority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No, no, no kind of authority. Just an ordinary, simple guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So there was some kind of hierarchy, then. There was a simple guard, and there would be a commander, because in one case you said, for instance, I think, that -- you informed when it was concerning, I think, Emsud. You said, "It was my duty to lock the dormitories, and I informed the duty officer about the absence of Bahonjic, and he informed the commander." So there was a hierarchy. We know what it means. You are a simple guard, you go to the superior, and the superior goes to other superior. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because in another time you said that nobody was superior to another. You were answering that to the Prosecutor. So what is the real, what is the real fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, look, it was like this: If there was some private business to attend to like when my mother was ill, then we would leave, whether they were angry at us leaving or not. I don't know if you can understand me there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm trying to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: We would leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You would leave without any permission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, because it was my mother's life at stake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: By the way, it was your mother's life at stake, and on the way you went to your lady friends. I mean, what -- so it was not a priority, really, to go to your mother. Did I --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, I went to them. My colleague stayed on, but I left straight away because my mother was my priority. We all love our mothers. I love her most of all in the whole wide world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, definitely, but perhaps the other lady friends had a priority. Now, I go back to Mr. Zigic. I think you said that he brought food and water in a minivan. Was that his duty? Was he, was he commissioned to bring food and water, or he brought it out of the goodness of his heart?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I think it was his duty. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was his duty. And he gave it to everyone, or he would favour certain people with it, only for some friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, he gave it to everybody. He didn't favourise, didn't have any favorites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was his duty, it was his function, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, I just wonder about the -- you said that the Rooms 3 and 4 were added after the attack on Prijedor and after what happened in Kozarac. But Room 1 and 2 existed before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: When I came, there was Room 1 and 2, and then later on Rooms 3 and 4 were added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Room 1 and 2 existed before the attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I don't understand. How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When was Room 1 and 2 created? When was the investigation introduced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I think it was after the attack on Prijedor and not before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Do you want me to clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would be really grateful.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I was at a checkpoint around Prijedor. It was called Hambarine, the checkpoint at Hambarine. I was not in Prijedor, so I really don't know when this was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good, that's enough as an answer. Now, concerning the night of the 24th of July, you went because it was an urgent call for your mother, and you left the compound at 21 hours. Until you left the compound, there was no sign of something happening? Everything was quiet, or was there some kind of movement and preparation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Everything was quiet. I couldn't notice anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And when you came back at 4.00 or 5.00 a.m., everything was already accomplished. You said you saw heaps, heaps of dead bodies, amounting to 15 [sic] corpses, and so on. Everything was already done when you came back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You did not see live, live action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No, I didn't, neither did I know how everything began. I really don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you said -- you also said that you could not -- as far as Mr. Zigic is concerned, he was not there, and you could have seen him or heard him if he was there. And you were mentioning that when you went, that there was a lot of commotion. Could, really, in this great noise and commotion, could you affirm surely that if he was there, you could have seen him or heard him, in the middle of this great -- call it what you want?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: As Zigic always liked to be the centre of attention, I would have had to have seen him and hear him. He is that kind of man, that kind of person. How can I explain this to you? Everything has to revolve around him. Everybody has to look at him. He must always be the centre of attraction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you could have, even if it was a big, what you say, killing and shooting and so on, you still could have heard him and seen him? You say you affirm that? Were you looking for him? You were not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, can I -- you used to drink sometimes with Mr. Zigic, but you said that it was better - and I'm just quoting you - "It was better to steer clear from him when he was drunk." What did he do when he was drunk? What was the danger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't like to be in his company, because then I would have to drink with him, and I don't drink as a rule; I don't drink alcohol as a rule. But if you were with him, he would make you drink. So when you were in his company, I would have to do something that I didn't actually want to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think you added that he would hit you or be friendly and you would never know; it's unpredictable. Did you see him hit anybody when he was drunk, committing any violence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I didn't see him hit anyone, but, you know, he would just give him a sort of slap on the neck like this. Perhaps you'll be able to understand me better if I show you. This gesture, sort of, in passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. At some answer -- in some answer you said, "I got order from my commander to call out two of the detainees to collect bodies onto a heap," I think it was Zlatan, Aco and Ajkic. You received orders. I want just to make sure that there was a discipline. That's right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: The commander, Zivko Knezevic, was there and he gave the order. He issued the orders. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you could still, in spite of this discipline, break the order and say, "I'm going away," any time. Can I understand this difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, yes. When he wasn't there, you could, because he was very strict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When he was there you could not go away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the night you left, he was not there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Witness DD/6, I also have a few questions for you. As regards Emsud Bahonjic, you indicated that there were persons who mistreated him. Do you have any idea as to who those individuals might be, those who used to mistreat him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to explain this to you. All kinds of people would come there, people that I didn't know. Some of them were very big, heavily built, and you have seen me. This was something that I could not prevent. And they were all armed. They could all open fire at any moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have partially answered my question. I was going to say -- I was going to ask who those persons were. Actually, you don't know them, you didn't know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to the evening of the 24th of July. You said that you had left the camp around 9.00, 9.30, and at about the same time the members of the Territorial Defence arrived. They must have arrived around that time. Did you actually see them come to the camp or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at one point in time the members of the TO were coming in and you were leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct, Your Honour. They had just arrived, and their leader was there in the hut when I took the keys back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speaking of the shooting incident, you told us that it had lasted for about one hour. I'm not sure that I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: What do you mean, one hour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one hour. As regards the incident involving 50 dead persons, the shooting lasted for about one hour. But maybe I misunderstood your words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I didn't say that the shooting lasted for about one hour. I don't know when it started and I don't know when it ended; I just know that it was all over when I came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I must have misunderstood your words, because it didn't actually make sense. Because if you had told me that it had lasted one hour, I would have probably had to ask you how you knew that. But I must have misunderstood your words. You also told us that Bahonjic was a dangerous person. You said that at least twice. Why did you say that? Why was he dangerous?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: Well, he was dangerous for them, not for me, but they considered him to be dangerous. I'm referring to my colleagues, the ones who were doing the same job. I didn't consider him to be dangerous. I didn't consider anyone to be dangerous, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what kind of danger could that be? How dangerous could he have been?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you just heard other people say that those individuals were dangerous, but you don't know anything about the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "No"; you mean you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have also told us that you woke up at around 4.00 a.m., that you woke up to the sound of shooting. Why do you say that it was 4.00 when you woke up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: It may have been sometime before that, but I went back between 4 and 5 a.m., and it probably took me only 15 minutes to get there, and it was already dawning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I would like to know why you said that it was 4.00 in the morning. Did you look at your watch? Did anyone tell you that it was 4.00? Why are you saying that it was 4.00?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DD/6
utterances.text: It was just my assumption because usually at that time it dawns in our area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much. You have answered my question. Witness DD/6, we have no further questions for you. You have answered a number of questions that have been put to you by both parties and the Judges. I would like to thank you for coming here to testify. I would like to wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence. I will ask the usher to take you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I also express my gratitude to the Court? It's really been a pleasure for me to testify before you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please do not move for a while. We have to draw down the blinds first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there are a couple of documents that need to be addressed. Ms. Somers, there have been no similar requests from the Defence, if I'm not mistaken. No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence of Mr. Zigic would like to tender this photograph into evidence. It is D9/4, that it be admitted as a Defence exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. D9/4 will be admitted into evidence. Ms. Somers, I think you, too, have some documents to tender.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would ask to have admitted into evidence 3/247, the solemn declaration; 3/248, the list of reserve police officers; 3/249, the official note signed by Sikirica. At this time, the Prosecution will not seek the admission of 3/250. It is part of a larger collection, and we will wait. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, any objections? Just a second, Mr. Simic. It has something to do with the document we're just discussing, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please wait for Mr. Deretic to state whether he has any objections or not. Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Zigic's Defence has no objections as to the admittance of the documents identified by 3/247, 3/248; however, we should like to express our reservations in respect of the document marked as 3/249 because the Defence has not been provided with the original of the document which is dated the 4th of July, 1992. So that is the reason why we object to this document being admitted into evidence as an official document of the Prosecution. As regards 3/250, I don't think I have to state my position on that because the Prosecutor doesn't seem to insist that this document also be admitted into evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Exhibits number 3/247, 3/248, exhibits of the Prosecution, will be admitted into evidence. Ms. Somers, do you wish to respond to Mr. Deretic as regards the document 3/249?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to earlier discussions between and amongst the Chamber and the parties, we are prepared to submit the declaration by the investigative official as to the origin and location of the document, and that should cover the nature of the reservation I believe was expressed. I do not have copies, but I would be happy to present -- I'm sorry, I do have copies. I have the original for the Chamber and copies for counsel. It will not have the exhibit number but will indicate the description of the document which is evident from the document itself. And if the Chamber wishes, I can have it, perhaps an "A" exhibit number marked with a breakdown of the new exhibit numbers that were given. May I ask the registrar, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or perhaps you can show the document to Mr. Deretic so that he can check the document himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The original -- at this time the original is in the evidence room. We would have to bring it down, but it is indicated on the declaration from where it was seized, and I think it has -- it should have the date. I have to check to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, that does not resolve the issue. I think it's better for you to meet with Mr. Deretic so that he can see the document today or next week, and then we will discuss it. We will spend far too much time trying to figure out whether it is okay for the document to be admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll just ask through the Chamber of counsel if Mr. Deretic will be here next week, I'm happy do it at his earliest convenience. He indicated the only reservation was as to seeing the original, whatever we have for an original, and I'm happy to do that as soon as he's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, do you want to reply to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Unfortunately, I will not be here next week, but I can tell you right away that the Defence of Mr. Zigic will at any rate oppose to the admittance of this official note for following reasons. First of all, it is an official note, and we still do not know whether Zoran Zigic was indeed interviewed, and we do not know the origin of the information which is contained in this official note. On the other hand, we also have problems with the date, the 4th of July, 1992. Later during our case, we will present a document regarding the whereabouts of Mr. Zigic at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I think that you will have the whole week to discuss the issue, and you can also then show the document to Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I certainly will do that, and if we need to present -- this is, of course, a new observation, it was not the initial one, but I will be very happy to present either a written submission if we need to, or just an oral one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So we will settle the issue involving document 3/249 at some later occasion. Mr. Simic, Krstan Simic, let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have only one objection regarding the document 3/248 and 3/249. In the heading of the document -- actually, of both documents, the translation doesn't seem to be accurate. As regards 3/248, the heading reads "RSM Prijedor II," and in the English version, in the brackets, the words which do not exist in the original have been added. The same goes for the document 3/249. Therefore, I should like to ask that the translation be brought in line with the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, 3/249 indicates a revised translation and the most recent pronouncement from the Language Services. So I'm not clear that Mr. Zigic -- Mr. Simic, excuse me, I beg your pardon, is on firm ground there. As to 3/248, I see that it appears to be a summary, and I would be very happy to resubmit this for a complete translation. It looks like it's in summary form because the names are in the original language and what was done, I see, is just showing the row -- the translation of the rows at the top. If the Chamber wishes a full translation, I am -- it would be no problem to have it done, just adopt the cell format, giving a translation of the top of each column and the general name of the document. If the Chamber wishes, I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the document number 3/249, the brackets were added in the English version. Those brackets do not exist in the original document, nor does the original document contain this wording. What I can read in the original is "RSM Prijedor II," and this is everything that we have here. We have the same words in the English translation, "RSM Prijedor II," plus we have the brackets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I think we've got lost. You mentioned the exhibit number 3/249, and now you're talking about 3/248. Where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have the same problem in both documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see. I'm sorry. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there is a portion of the text which has been added in the English translation and which does not exist in the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What is the text that you're talking about, the added text?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the brackets in 3/248, and the same brackets in 3/249, in the heading of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. But, Mr. Simic, as regards 3/248, you don't want the names and the dates to be translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I just wanted to draw your attention to the mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Simic. Thank you. Ms. Somers, there seems to be a certain doubt, which can be justified, in my opinion. Perhaps you should submit these once again to the Translation Unit with the objection made by Mr. Simic, and then afterwards we will be able to admit the document into evidence. We will mark it with an "A." What do you think of it, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so there should be no doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you very much, Mr. Simic, for your assistance. I think that we will be able to come up with an accurate version in the end. I don't think that there's anything else that needs to be addressed today. If I'm not mistaken, we will see each other again on the 9th in order to continue Mr. Zigic's Defence case. But I can see Mr. Stojanovic on his feet. Mr. Stojanovic, what can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. You're quite right. Our next date is the 9th of April. However, I have to tell you what else is on our agenda. We only have three working days that week, and according to our plans, we were -- we intended to hear five witnesses, which is far too many, because I don't think that we will have enough time. Speaking of the decision of the Chamber to call three witnesses who were initially scheduled as Prosecution witnesses concerning that particular week and that particular time, I don't think that we will be able to deal with all those during that week. The week after, in view of the holidays and the decision of the video conferencing, is also very problematic. Your Honours, I think that we will only have Tuesday and Friday as our trial days, that is, the 17th and the 20th of April, because the 16th is a day off. We will have some protected witnesses as well, and I don't think that we will be able to involve the Witnesses and Victims Protection Unit, who do not work on weekends, so we will have problems with bringing the witnesses here. Then there will be a long break for them because of the videolink. And I think, and through no fault of ours, I think that we will not be able to use many days during that period of time, because we have some four or five days off, holidays, that is. We also have the fourth week, from the 23rd to the 27th, and we wanted to hear expert witnesses during that week. We have a graphologist, a forensic medicine specialist, and perhaps also a psychologist that we want to examine during that week. Perhaps one of the witnesses could be moved; however, it is my concern that in view of the holidays and the fact that we have a videolink testimony, and also in view of my colleagues, it will be very difficult for us to organise ourselves, especially with respect to the Victims and Witnesses Protection Unit. So I would like to know whether there is any possibility of moving the videolink one day ahead or later. I know it's a big problem, but I don't know about the preparations, in what stage they are at this point, for the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, you mentioned a week with three working days. I don't know what week you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's our next term, that is, the 9th, the 10th, and the 11th of April. There is a Plenary Session scheduled for the 12th of April, and on the 13th there is the Good Friday. It's a holiday here. We scheduled five witnesses for those days, but I don't know whether it will be possible, because the Easter holidays stretch over to the 16th, which is also part of the week which actually belongs to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, but at the time we were drafting the schedule, we were perfectly aware of the fact that the week does not have five working days. There's one other matter that we have to take into consideration. I don't know. Perhaps Ms. Mackintosh could tell us something more about the possibility of moving the video conference in order to facilitate things. LEGAL OFFICER: Yes. I spoke to the Victims and Witnesses Unit, who indicated that for Mr. Stojanovic's witnesses to testify on Tuesday, the 17th, they will have to travel on the Thursday before Easter, which is rather inconvenient with them. The registry is prepared to move the videolink forward a day, for the 17th and 18th, so that your witnesses could be heard on the Thursday and Friday of that week. I mentioned it to the Prosecution, and they were going to get back to me on whether they will also be able to accommodate that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I respond to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Somers will respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. At the beginning of the session, Your Honour, we did inform Ms. Mackintosh that I have spoken with our representatives, who will be travelling to the videolink, and they are willing to shuffle their schedule around to accommodate this need. So yes, so that they will be up and running for the 17th and 18th for videolink. I do have one other point I would like to ask, whenever the Chamber will allow me, on one of the representations made by Mr. Stojanovic about witnesses, so if I may have a direction from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I think that as regards the possibility of moving the videolink forward a day, we do not have a problem with that; at least, the Chamber doesn't have a problem with that. But I may be lost. Was there anything else that you wished to address, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. There was a mention on page - let me just see - 92, line 17 and 18, about Court witnesses, and I distinctly recall a discussion that we had earlier that the witnesses referred to were not Court witnesses but rather Defence witnesses, on whose behalf, I believe, there was an order issued by this Chamber, but they are not Court witnesses under Rule 98. That was my understanding, and I just wanted to have clarification so we would know how to approach those witnesses should they, in fact, come. The Defence had some difficulty in commanding the presence of persons who had been listed as Prosecution witnesses and asked for an order from the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't ask for the presence of that witness on behalf of the Chamber pursuant to Article [as interpreted] 98, no. We only summoned the witness to appear. But for the Defence, you have the decision of the 16th of March this year, which I believe is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, and therefore I was concerned when Mr. Stojanovic said, "Speaking of the decision of the Chamber to call three witnesses who were initially scheduled as Prosecution witnesses ..." I wanted to make quite sure that I did understand the Chamber's order and that they are Defence witnesses -- that the Defence is seeking the assistance of the Chamber in commanding their presence as Defence witnesses. They are not called by the Chamber. And that was what I was hoping for clarification on from the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood it well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is only one point. Just so that the Chamber knows, we do not have an order, an exact confirmed order of witnesses, and if Mr. Stojanovic would be kind enough, before the close of business today, to give that to us so we can be ready for the next set of witnesses, we would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. You wish to reply to Ms. Somers? Is there anything else that you wish to bring up before we finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As regards our obligations, I believe that we were quite fair, even more fair than the other side. We provided them with the appropriate information 15 days ahead. I must admit that I learned about some Prosecution witnesses on the day they were supposed to testify. We have provided the list 10 or 15 days ahead of time. The way I understand your list, the time frame is seven days ahead. I believe I have done even more than that. I still haven't provided the information for the third group, but I don't think it is proper at this time for the Prosecution to insist. We still have too many current problems that we have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, thank you very much. What are your other issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I think that if we move the videolink forward a day, I think it would be helpful for us, but I really don't see how we will be able to start on the 9th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, if the registry tells us that it is possible, that is how the Chamber will rule. What are the other questions that you want to address?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, I have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No. I will ask Mr. Stojanovic privately about the order of the witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You could have done it already. So we will have a one-week break and then we will resume. I hope you will be able to find an agreement as regards technical matters. If you have any doubts, any problems, please contact Ms. Mackintosh who can always notify us of any technical issues that need to be dealt with. We do not have anything else to discuss? Yes Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted you to finish with the routine matters. As you know, and it would be well to remind ourselves, at one point of the testimony of Mr. Delic who was a Defence witness for Radic, the question arose as to two terms used. One was the "razvodnik straze" term, guard shift leader, "razvodnik straze"; and the second was the shift leader, "sef smjene." So those two terms. I have received, and I will inform Ms. Somers, a memorandum which the Translation Service sent to you. The problem was contained in the following: What Ms. Somers read out was what she asked. Then in the B/C/S, it was translated differently. Ms. Somers asked, "What is a shift leader?" And in the B/C/S, the interpretation of that which was given to Mr. Delic was "razvodnik straze," and in the memo, they put that right now, a correction. However, a problem remains. This is a quotation given by Ms. Somers. She was quoting me, my question. Ms. Somers was quoting me and my question to Mr. Delic whether any shift leaders existed, and that he said no, that his answer was no. However, what I asked him was, did the razvodnik straze exist, and he said no, meaning guard shift leader. Now, Ms. Somers quoted what she saw appearing on the screen, and now we have a problem. What is the value of everything that -- the worth of everything that has entered into the LiveNote? Ms. Somers would not have quoted me incorrectly because she doesn't do that; and secondly, she was quoting what she had seen on the screen as being my words. Now I am asking myself whether we ought to put the previous section right, too, which brings me to two questions: Is the Trial Chamber aware of the problem in its entirety, which is very worrying for me; and what is the value of everything recorded on that particular page of the transcript? How do we assess its worth? So, do I call witness Delic again to testify, or will the Trial Chamber make another decision? I don't mind, but we must clear this matter up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fila. Thank you for bringing up that question. It is perhaps my fault, but yes, the memo did reach me from the Translation Service, but there were certain developments which I was not abreast of. So perhaps I will see how matters stand, and when we take our work up again next week, I'll inform you of how the situation stands and what we're going to do. Either we're going to recall the witness Mr. Delic - that was my first reaction; if he was available, that's what I said first - or the other possibility is that I think that we all more or less agree that there was some of this difficulty in the translation and interpretation which shifted the answers around. So we shall take that up and we'll give you an answer, Mr. Fila, in due course. Is that all right? I hope so. And having said that, we're going to adjourn for the weekend and next week's work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
